Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson is doubling down on buying the selloff after the S&P 500 broke below his 7,100 downside target. In Monday's note, his team called it "the fat pitch we have patiently been waiting for, and we're not going to miss it," adding that "markets bottom on bad news and deleveraging. We have had a lot of both" (via Bloomberg).

How we got here:

▪️ In late September, he warned of a drop to as low as 7,100 before the bull market resumed.
▪️ In early November, he said the correction was in its final innings, with a 7,100 to 7,300 range. On November 16, he raised his 12-month target to 8,700.
▪️ On Friday, the S&P 500 closed at 6,910.39, 2.7% below the bottom of that range and 11.6% below the October 6 record. That capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest since February 2020.

Why he's pressing the call rather than backing off:

▪️ He calls the break below his range an overshoot of fair value, driven by forced deleveraging. His team is more bullish tactically than at any time since early April.
▪️ Sentiment: his sentiment indicator hit −1.6 and the VIX hit 36, both matching December 2018, and hedge fund positioning is similarly washed out.
▪️ Valuation: the S&P 500's forward P/E has dropped from nearly 23 in late October to 16.5, below its 17.4 long-run average. The Nasdaq 100 is under 17, below its pandemic low.
▪️ Earnings: by his math, stocks are pricing in about a 6% drop in 2027 earnings. He forecasts 14% growth, and consensus is 17%.
▪️ He likes hyperscalers, industrials, quality cyclicals with improving estimates, and companies benefiting from AI adoption.
▪️ The main risk is still a hawkish Fed. But he thinks market pricing is "far too hawkish" and expects a calmer message in December than some fear.

The history backs him, with a catch. Since 1990, the VIX has had 17 episodes where it first closed at 35 or higher (Friday's close was 35.89):

▪️ The S&P 500 was higher 12 months later in 14 of the 17, with a median gain of 21.6%. That compares with 11.9% for any 12-month stretch since 1990.
▪️ December 2018, the episode he compares this one to, was followed by a 37.1% gain.
▪️ But the first spike often wasn't the low. In 8 of the 17, the S&P 500 fell more than 5% further within three months, including another 34.9% in 2008 and 24.9% in 2020.
▪️ The three losing years were 2001 and 2008, both earnings recessions, and 2022, a Fed hiking cycle.

History would indicate his call should hold unless earnings roll over or the Fed gets much more aggressive. The market is already pricing in an earnings drop he doesn't expect, so the bigger swing factor is the Fed, the one risk he concedes. 

Morgan Stanley chief economist Seth Carpenter acknowledged in his Sunday Start note (via ZeroHedge) that clients pushed back hard on the bank's "Embracing Risk" outlook, and that even if the bank is right, the path through 2027 "will not be smooth or linear."

Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson (Strategy Data Pack, Friday) says the S&P 500 “catching down” to weaker breadth “is likely the final stage of this correction," after he rightly called a continuation of the pullback in semi's in the event of a big Democratic victory.

But he isn’t calling the bottom yet: “We are getting close, but would like to see… further confirmation from our sentiment indicator.” His year-end target stays 8,000.

Here's what’s happened to the three “clearing events” he laid out last weekend:

▪️ Midterms: Democrats took both chambers, with at least 54 Senate seats. Wilson had said a 52-48 Senate was priced in but 55-45 wasn’t, and that a bigger margin could fuel pushback on data centers, so he nailed that.
▪️ AI and semis: Thursday was the S&P’s worst day since April 2025 (−4.4%) and the Nasdaq-100’s worst since March 2020 (−6.4%). The SOX fell about 12% on weak chip guidance and fears of data-center rules after the election. That left it down about 19% from October 26, when Wilson called for another 10% to 15% drop into mid-November, another hit.
▪️ Liquidity, the one he ranks most important, hasn’t cleared. He says Fed Chair Warsh acknowledged financial conditions are doing some of the Fed’s tightening but wouldn’t call them “tight,” so the bar for a dovish pivot “remains high.” Then Friday’s payrolls (+165,000 vs. ~65,000 expected) pushed December hike odds to about 78%.

The math from Friday’s close of 7,376.86 (−5.7% from the record, −2.7% on the week):
▪️ 7,100 to 7,200 is another 2.4% to 3.8% down.
▪️ 8,000 is +8.4% from here. His 12-month base case is 8,300 (+12.5%), with a 5,900 bear case and 9,400 bull case.

On the catch-down, as he also indicated was likely, the average stock is holding up better than the index:
▪️ Thursday, the equal-weight S&P fell 2.9% vs. 4.4% for the cap-weighted index.
▪️ In October, equal-weight beat cap-weight by 5.9 points, the second-widest monthly gap since 2003.
▪️ Wilson notes median Russell 3000 earnings growth is running 14%, the strongest in four years.

His sentiment indicator was at −0.75 as of Thursday. That compares with roughly −1.45 at the Iran-war low earlier this year and about −2.1 on Liberation Day.

US net equity inflows are up to ~3.0% of GDP, their highest on record in data going back to the 1980s.

Net equity inflows measure foreign purchases of US stocks minus US investors' purchases of foreign equities.

This figure has risen nearly +5.0 percentage points since the 2022 bear market low.

Meanwhile, net debt inflows, which measure foreign purchases of US debt securities, such as Treasuries minus US purchases of foreign debt securities, are down to ~1.8%, their lowest since 2022.

As a result, net equity inflows have surpassed net debt inflows as a % of GDP by the widest margin since the 2008 Financial Crisis.

In other words, foreign investors are increasingly directing money towards US equities rather than US bonds.

Overseas demand for US equities has never been this strong.

I don't think there's ever been a more important time to be an investor than today.

And yet, investing presents a strange paradox.

On one hand, it's never been easier. With a smartphone and a few clicks, you can invest in almost anything.

On the other, knowing what to do has never been harder.

I've spent more than 15 years in financial markets, and I've never seen so much information, commentary and opinion competing for investors' attention. Somewhere in all that noise, you're supposed to figure out what actually matters.

Everything I've learned in my career has gone into my answer to that:

MACROSHARK
